title: Each Customer's Favourite Product With LATERAL
outcome: 🆕 new practice question — not attempted yet
watchOutFor: LATERAL lets the subquery refer to c.customer_id; CROSS JOIN drops customers with no orders.
problem: The CRM team wants to personalise emails with each customer's most-bought product.
objective: For every customer who has ordered, show the product they bought the most units of (ties broken by product name) and the units, highest first.
expectedOutput:
| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| customer_id | Customer |
| company_name | Company |
| product_name | Most-bought product |
| units | Units of that product |

| customer_id | company_name | product_name | units |
|-------------|--------------|--------------|-------|
| BOLID | Bólido Comidas preparadas | Inlagd Sill | 47 |
| BLONP | Blondesddsl père et fils | Rössle Sauerkraut | 43 |
| GOURL | Gourmet Lanchonetes | Rogede sild | 40 |
| GREAL | Great Lakes Food Market | Chartreuse verte | 40 |

*(Sample rows are illustrative — the first few rows from the practice dataset, shown to convey shape/format; your data instance may differ.)*
approach:
1. FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (subquery).
2. The subquery sums units per product for c.customer_id, orders by units DESC, product_name, LIMIT 1.
3. Order the result by units, then customer_id.
mySolution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name, top.product_name, top.units
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.product_name, SUM(d.quantity) AS units
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_details d ON d.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products p ON p.product_id = d.product_id
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    GROUP BY p.product_name
    ORDER BY units DESC, p.product_name
    LIMIT 1
) AS top
ORDER BY top.units DESC, c.customer_id;
solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name, top.product_name, top.units
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.product_name, SUM(d.quantity) AS units
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_details d ON d.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products p ON p.product_id = d.product_id
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    GROUP BY p.product_name
    ORDER BY units DESC, p.product_name
    LIMIT 1
) AS top
ORDER BY top.units DESC, c.customer_id;
referenceQuery:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name, top.product_name, top.units
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.product_name, SUM(d.quantity) AS units
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_details d ON d.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products p ON p.product_id = d.product_id
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    GROUP BY p.product_name
    ORDER BY units DESC, p.product_name
    LIMIT 1
) AS top
ORDER BY top.units DESC, c.customer_id;
why: A LATERAL subquery runs once per outer row and can use that row's columns, which makes 'top N per group' direct: sort inside the subquery and take LIMIT 1. CROSS JOIN LATERAL keeps only customers for whom the subquery returns a row, i.e. customers with orders; LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true would keep the others with NULLs.
pitfalls: Leaving out LATERAL: a plain subquery in FROM can't see c.customer_id.
No tie-breaker in the inner ORDER BY, which makes the chosen product depend on the plan.
Using LEFT JOIN LATERAL without ON true (it requires an ON clause).

followups.question: How would you return the top 3 products per customer?
followups.answer: Change LIMIT 1 to LIMIT 3; the outer query then has up to three rows per customer.

followups.question: What's the window-function alternative?
followups.answer: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY units DESC, product_name) over a grouped CTE, keeping rn = 1.

followups.question: When is LATERAL faster?
followups.answer: When an index lets each inner query stop after a few rows, for example top-N by date with an index on (customer_id, order_date).

takeaway: LATERAL is a per-row subquery in FROM: the cleanest way to write top-N per group.
